'''Manute Bol''' ({{IPAc-en|m|ə|ˈ|n|uː|t|_|ˈ|b|oʊ|l}} {{respell|mə|NOOT|_|BOHL}}; died June 19, 2010) was a South Sudanese-American professional [[basketball]] player and political [[activist]]. Listed at {{height|ft=7|in=6}}<ref name="MBNBA"/> or {{height|ft=7|in=7}}<ref name="NBAencyc"/> tall, Bol was one of the two [[List of tallest players in NBA history|tallest players]] in the history of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA).

After he played [[college basketball]] for the [[Bridgeport Purple Knights]], Bol was selected by the [[Washington Bullets]] in the [[1985 NBA draft]]. Bol played for the Bullets and three other teams over the course of his NBA career, which lasted from 1985 to 1995. A [[center (basketball)|center]], Bol is considered among the best shot-blockers in the history of the sport and is the only NBA player to retire with more career blocked shots than points scored. {{As of|2026|March}}, he ranked second in NBA history in [[block (basketball)|blocked shots]] per game and 17th in [[List of National Basketball Association career blocks leaders|total blocked shots]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/blk_career.html|title=NBA & ABA Career Leaders and Records for Blocks|website=[[Basketball Reference]]|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|accessdate=28 March 2026}}</ref>

Bol was notable for his efforts to promote human rights in his native Sudan and aid for Sudanese refugees.

==Early life== 
Manute Bol was born to Madut and Okwok Bol in [[Turalei]], a small village in what was at the time [[Sudan]], now part of [[South Sudan]].<ref name="Washington Post">{{cite news|last=Hedges|first=Chris|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1989/06/28/no-bol-of-cherries-for-manutes-family/d76dd2a2-ba8f-4e38-a209-5a2b84641ab0/|title=No Bol Of Cherries For Manute's Family|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=June 27, 1989|accessdate=March 11, 2025}}</ref> His father was a tribal elder for the [[Dinka people]].<ref name="Washington Post"/> Before his birth, Okwok had twice given birth to [[stillbirth|stillborn]] twins, and upon a visit to the local mystic, was promised a healthy boy who was to be named Manute.<ref name="Washington Post"/> In the [[Dinka language]], Manute means "special blessing".<ref name="Atavist">{{cite web|last=Conn|first=Jordan|url=https://magazine.atavist.com/the-defender/|title=The Defender|website=[[Atavist Magazine]]|date=n.d.|accessdate=March 11, 2025}}</ref> Bol's exact birth year is unknown; the birth date listed in his [[USCIS immigration forms|United States immigration forms]] is October 16, 1962, although [[Cleveland State Vikings men's basketball|Cleveland State basketball]] head coach [[Kevin Mackey]] claims he chose this date to appease immigration officials.<ref name="NYDN birthday">{{cite web|last1=Anderson|first1=Stefan|title=Manute Bol lied about his age, may have been 50 years old when he played in the NBA: report|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/basketball/manute-bol-lied-age-50-played-nba-article-1.3649488|website=NY Daily News|access-date=November 22, 2017|date=November 21, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Yahoo Birthdate">{{cite web|last=Rohrbach|first=Ben|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/manute-bols-birthday-allegedly-made-mightve-played-age-50-220526309.html|title=Manute Bol's birthday was allegedly made up, and he might've played at age 50|website=[[Yahoo Sports]]|date=November 21, 2017|accessdate=March 11, 2025}}</ref> Mackey said, "I wanted to make sure he was young enough because he didn't have an age. I think he was [in his 40s], I really do. But there's no way of ever really knowing."<ref>{{cite web|last=Maloney|first=Jack|url=https://www.cbssports.com/nba/news/ex-coach-says-he-made-up-manute-bols-birthday-he-couldve-been-40-or-50-in-nba/|title=Ex-coach says he made up Manute Bol's birthday: He could've been '40 or 50' in NBA|website=[[CBS Sports]]|date=November 22, 2017|accessdate=March 11, 2025}}</ref> Former teammate [[Jayson Williams]] believes Bol may have been as old as 55 before he retired in 1995, potentially placing his year of birth as early as 1940.<ref name="Yahoo Birthdate"/>

Bol grew up during a period of relative peace in Sudan, a country that had recently experienced a lengthy [[First Sudanese Civil War|civil war]].<ref name="Atavist"/> This allowed him to avoid military service and experience a normal life.<ref name="Atavist"/> At the time, the Dinka people did not encourage formal education, and Bol instead helped raise livestock.<ref>{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|pages=51–54|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> An often repeated story about Bol's life in Sudan was that he killed a lion with a spear, although former teammate [[Charles Barkley]] has questioned the validity of the story.<ref name="Atavist"/> As Bol grew older, he was expected to participate in a ritual in which young boys would have some of their teeth removed with a chisel and have incisions cut into their forehead, which would signal one's ascension to manhood.<ref name="Book 54-55">{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|pages=54–55|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> Bol did not want to partake in the ritual and instead wanted an education, and on two separate instances ran away from home.<ref name="Book 54-55"/> In the second instance, he lived in [[Babanusa]] for about a year but struggled in school since he barely understood [[Arabic]].<ref name="Book 54-55"/> Once he returned to Turalei, he participated in the ritual.<ref name="Book 54-55"/>

Bol came from a family of extraordinarily tall men and women.<ref name="NYT Death">{{cite web|last=McGeehan|first=Patrick|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/20/sports/basketball/20bol.html|title=Manute Bol, N.B.A. Player and Activist, Dies at 47|website=[[The New York Times]]|date=June 19, 2010|accessdate=March 11, 2025}}</ref> His mother was {{height|ft=6|in=10}}, his father was {{height|ft=6|in=8}}, his sister was {{height|ft=6|in=8}}, and his great-grandfather was {{height|ft=7|in=10}}.<ref name="NYT Death"/> The Dinka belong to a larger ethnic group known as the [[Nilotic peoples|Nilotes]], which are among the [[Average human height by country|tallest populations in the world]].<ref>{{cite journal |last = Roberts |first = D. F. |author2=D. R. Bainbridge |title = Nilotic physique |journal = Am. J. Phys. Anthropol. |volume = 21 |issue = 3 |pages = 341–70 |date = Sep 1963 |doi = 10.1002/ajpa.1330210309 |pmid = 14159970 }}</ref> Bol recalled, "I was born in a village where you cannot measure yourself".<ref name="harrowing"/> By his late teens, Bol was {{height|ft=7|in=7}}.<ref name="Atavist"/><ref name="harrowing"/> Unlike most people of extreme height, Bol did not suffer from a growth-related pathological disorder such as [[gigantism]].<ref name="harrowing">{{cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-2002-03-31-0203310024-story.html|title=For Manute Bol, a Harrowing Comeback|first=Lynne|last=Tuohy|website=[[Hartford Courant]]|date=March 31, 2002|access-date=February 7, 2019}}</ref> In 1979, a photographer for a newspaper in [[Khartoum]] took a photo of Bol.<ref name="Book 55-57">{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|pages=55–57|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> The image was widely circulated, and the police chief in [[Wau, South Sudan|Wau]] invited him to play for the police basketball team.<ref name="Book 55-57"/> Bol initially declined as he did not understand the appeal of the game, but was eventually convinced by one of his cousins.<ref name="Book 55-57"/> When Bol tried to [[Slam dunk|dunk]] for the first time, he knocked out two of his upper teeth on the [[Rim (basketball)|rim]], and resolved to practice more so as to avoid another injury.<ref name="Book 55-57"/>

After a few games in Wau, Bol was recruited to play for a Catholic team in Khartoum.<ref>{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|page=57|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> His coach instructed him to focus on [[Block (basketball)|blocking]] and [[Rebound (basketball)|rebounding]], and whenever he was not on the court, he was to watch how the taller players would position themselves underneath the basket for [[layup]]s and dunks.<ref name="Book 74">{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|page=74|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> Bol's height made him near impossible to guard, and it helped the Catholic team become one of the best teams in the league.<ref name="Book 74"/> Bol also joined the [[Sudan men's national basketball team]], and played games in various African and European countries.<ref name="Book 74–75">{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|pages=74–75|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref> A requirement to play for the national team was to enlist in the military, and Bol was listed as a [[paratrooper]], but never saw any service time.<ref name="Book 74–75"/> Around this period, Bol watched footage of [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) games, and dreamed of playing in the United States.<ref name="Book 75"/> When the national team was scheduled to play a game in [[Fort Bragg]], [[North Carolina]], Bol was not included on the roster, and concluded that the team was worried he would defect to the United States.<ref name="Book 75">{{cite book|last=Montville|first=Leigh|title=Manute : The Center of Two Worlds|publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]]|year=1993|page=75|isbn=0-671-74928-5}}</ref>

===Move to the United States===
Coach [[Don Feeley]], formerly the basketball coach at [[Fairleigh Dickinson University]] in [[New Jersey]], traveled to Sudan to coach and held clinics for the Sudanese national team in 1982. Feeley convinced Bol to go to the United States and play basketball.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.answers.com/topic/manute-bol|title=Answers – The Most Trusted Place for Answering Life's Questions|website=Answers.com|access-date=27 August 2017}}</ref><ref name="auto1">{{cite web|url=https://plus2clothing.com/happened-manute-bol/|title=What Happened to Manute Bol|first=Steve|last=Rogers|date=7 April 2016|website=Plus 2 Clothing}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=February 2024}}

With Feeley's input, Bol first landed in [[Cleveland]]. According to [[Cleveland State University]] basketball coach [[Kevin Mackey]], Bol could not provide a record of his birth date.<ref name="Yahoo Birthdate"/> Mackey listed it as October 16, 1962, on Cleveland State documents, making Bol 19 years old, but he believed Bol was actually much older, possibly as old as 35.<ref name="Yahoo Birthdate"/> Bol did not speak or write English at the time of his arrival in Cleveland. He improved his English skills after months of classes at ESL Language Centers at [[Case Western Reserve University]], but not enough to qualify for enrollment at Cleveland State. Bol never played a game for Cleveland State. Five years later, Cleveland State was placed on two years' probation for providing improper financial assistance to Bol and two other African players.<ref>{{cite news |last = Associated Press |title = Penalties Upheld for Cleveland State |newspaper = The New York Times |date = Apr 22, 1988 |url = https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=940DE6D9173AF931A15757C0A96E948260 }}</ref><ref name="auto2">{{cite web|url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/fl-xpm-1985-02-20-8501060790-story.html|title=THE KING DINKA DUNKER: 7–6 HERDSMAN TO NBA?|first=Mitch |last=Albom|website=Sun-Sentinel.com|date=February 20, 1985 }}</ref>

Again with Feeley's influence, Bol declared his intention to play professionally in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). The [[Los Angeles Clippers|San Diego Clippers]] drafted him in the [[1983 NBA draft]] as the 97th overall pick. Clippers head coach [[Jim Lynam]] received a call about Bol from Feeley, whom he knew from coaching circles. "So, I said, 'Have you told anyone else about this?'" Lynam recalled. "Feeley said the only one in the NBA he had called was [[Frank Layden]] at Utah. He said Frank said he couldn't take another big guy like this. He already had [[Mark Eaton]]. I was the second guy Feeley had called. I told him he didn't have to call anyone else."<ref name="auto3">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1990/12/17/123285/a-tall-story-manute-bol-the-sixers-7-ft7-in-center-views-life-from-a-unique-perspective|title=A TALL STORY|first=Leigh|last=Montville|magazine=Sports Illustrated|date=December 17, 1990}}</ref>

After the June 1983 draft, Lynam traveled to Cleveland and watched Bol play pickup games. In speaking with Bol, through a fellow Sudanese player, Lynam learned that he had become hesitant about playing professionally because he did not know the language well enough to understand coaches. Lynam said, "One of the things everyone was looking at was his passport. His passport said he was 19 years old. His passport also said he was five feet two." When Lynam asked Bol about the discrepancy between his real height and his passport height, Bol said he had been sitting down when measured by Sudan officials.<ref name="auto3"/>

Language and passport concerns were set aside when the NBA ruled that Bol had not been eligible for the draft as he had not declared 45 days before the draft as required and declared the pick invalid.<ref name="USAToday">{{cite news|title=Scouts: Bol has slim chance at success|date=April 12, 1985|first=Kathy|last=Blumenstock|newspaper=[[USA Today]]}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=September 2019}}

==College basketball career==
[[File:Manute Bol playing at Bridgeport 1984.jpg|thumb|Bol ''(left)'' playing for [[Bridgeport Purple Knights]] in 1984]]
With the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA) questioning his eligibility for [[NCAA Division I]] basketball, Bol enrolled at the [[University of Bridgeport]], an [[NCAA Division II]] school with an English program for foreign students. He played for the [[Bridgeport Purple Knights|Purple Knights]] in the 1984–85 season. His coach was [[Bruce Webster]], a friend of Feeley. Bol averaged 22.5 points, 13.5 rebounds, and 7.1 blocks per game for the Purple Knights. The team, which previously drew 500–600 spectators, routinely sold out the 1,800-seat gym.<ref name="USAToday"/> With Bol, Bridgeport qualified for the [[1985 NCAA Division II men's basketball tournament]].<ref name="auto2"/>

==Professional basketball career==
Bol turned professional in May 1985, signing with the [[Rhode Island Gulls]] of the spring [[United States Basketball League]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/05/17/sports/sports-people-bol-may-turn-pro.html|title=SPORTS PEOPLE; Bol May Turn Pro|newspaper=The New York Times|date=17 May 1985}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-07-07-sp-9482-story.html|title=Unusual Gulls Are Favorite in This Town|agency=Associated Press|date=7 July 1985|via=LA Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.si.com/vault/1985/06/24/628058/a-taste-of-high-society|title=A Taste Of High Society|first=Bruce|last=Newman|magazine=Sports Illustrated |date=June 24, 1985}}</ref> Going into the [[1985 NBA draft]], scouts believed that Bol needed another year or two of college; however, Bol opted for the draft because he felt it was the only way to earn enough money to get his sister out of Sudan, which was in [[Democratic Republic of the Sudan#Unrest and coup|a state of political unrest]] at the time.<ref name="USAToday"/>

===Washington Bullets (1985–1988) ===
The [[Washington Bullets]] drafted Bol in the second round with the 31st overall selection.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

When he arrived in the United States, Bol weighed {{convert|180|lb|kg}}<ref>{{cite news |last = Epting |first = Chris |title = The Manute We Knew: Curious, Shy, One of the Family . . . and a Lion Slayer |newspaper = AOL News |date = Jun 24, 2010 |url = http://www.aolnews.com/2010/06/24/the-manute-we-knew-curious-shy-one-of-the-family/ |archive-url = https://archive.today/20130117040047/http://www.aolnews.com/2010/06/24/the-manute-we-knew-curious-shy-one-of-the-family/ |url-status = dead |archive-date = January 17, 2013 }}</ref> and had gained just under {{convert|20|lb|kg}} by the time he entered the NBA. The Bullets sent Bol to strength training with [[University of Maryland]] coach Frank Costello, where he could initially lift only {{convert|44|lb|kg}} on 10-repetition [[bench press]] and {{convert|55|lb|kg}} on 10-repetition [[squat (exercise)|squat]]<ref>{{cite magazine |last = McCallum |first = Jack |title = Welcome To 'Air Bol': Stronger and heavier, the Bullets' 7'7" Manute Bol could be a force |magazine = Sports Illustrated |date = Oct 21, 1985 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1120035/ |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130326041929/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1120035 |url-status = dead |archive-date = March 26, 2013 }}</ref> (his [[body mass index]] was 15.3 and he initially had a 31" (80 cm) waist).<ref>{{cite news |last = McManis |first = Sam |title = At 7 Foot 6, Manute Bol of Sudan Is Surely Rangy Enough for America's City Game and He Has Talent, but at 190 Pounds He May Not Be Strong Enough for Big Time: Basketball's Tallest Story |newspaper = Los Angeles Times |date = Feb 11, 1985 |url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-02-11-sp-4394-story.html }}</ref>

Bol's first tenure with the Bullets lasted three seasons, from 1985 to 1988. In his rookie season ([[1985–86 NBA season|1985–1986]]), he appeared in 80 games and recorded a career-high 5.0 blocks per game. That year, during his first career start on December 12, Bol set a Washington franchise record with 12 blocks and scored a career high 18 points in a 110–108 overtime victory against the [[Milwaukee Bucks]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Bullets, Bol Stop Bucks In Overtime |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1985/12/13/bullets-bol-stop-bucks-in-overtime/75ee30da-6a60-40b3-bbbc-33d1b1f352f6/ |newspaper=Washington Post |date=December 13, 1985}}</ref> His total of 397 blocks set the NBA rookie record and remains the second-highest single-season total in league history, behind [[Mark Eaton]]'s 456 in 1984–85.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_1986_leaders.html|title=1985–86 NBA Leaders|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/blk_season.html|title=NBA & ABA Single Season Leaders and Records for Blocks|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref> Bol led the league with 5.0 blocks per game during the 1985–86 season.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol was named to the NBA All-Defensive Second Team in 1986.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star-1986-nba-all-defen/5883809/|title=1986 NBA All-Defensive Team voting (Maximum points: 44)|work=The Indianapolis Star |date=April 25, 1986|pages=37|via=newspapers.com}}</ref>

In 1987, the Bullets drafted the {{height|ft=5|in=3}} [[point guard]] [[Muggsy Bogues]], pairing the tallest and shortest players in the league on the court for one season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/07/13/NBA-Bullets-Welcome-Manute-Bol-7-6/6670490075200/|title=NBA Bullets Welcome Manute Bol, 7–6|website=UPI|date=July 13, 1985}}</ref><ref name="basketball-reference.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01.html|title=Manute Bol Stats|website=Basketball-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |date=October 8, 2014 |title=The NBA's Tallest and Shortest Together |url=https://www.si.com/nba/photos/2014/10/08/nbas-tallest-and-shortest-together |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219171737/https://www.si.com/nba/photos/2014/10/08/nbas-tallest-and-shortest-together |archive-date=February 19, 2015 |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]]}}</ref>

Bol competed in the NBA playoffs with the Bullets in 1986, 1987, and 1988.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

===Golden State Warriors (1988–1990)===
On June 8, 1988, the Bullets traded Bol to the [[Golden State Warriors]] for [[Dave Feitl]] and a 1989 second round draft pick ([[Doug Roth]] was later selected).<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol's first tenure with the Warriors lasted two seasons, from 1988 to 1990. In his first season with Golden State, he attempted three-point shots with regularity. In that season he attempted a career-high 91 three-pointers and made 20 of them. During this time, he may have helped to popularize the expression "[[wikt:my bad|my bad]]", although a 2005 suggestion that he coined the phrase has been discounted.<ref name="Pullum">{{cite web|url=http://itre.cis.upenn.edu/~myl/languagelog/archives/002693.html|title=Language Log: Pick-up basketballism reaches Ivy League faculty vocabulary|last=Pullum|first=Geoffrey K. |author-link=Geoff Pullum |date=7 December 2005|access-date=2010-06-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.visualthesaurus.com/cm/wordroutes/2327/|title=The Manute Bol Theory of "My Bad"|last=Zimmer|first=Ben |author-link=Ben Zimmer |date=22 June 2010|work=Word Routes|publisher=Thinkmap Visual Thesaurus|access-date=2010-06-23}}</ref>

Bol led the league with 4.3 blocks per game for the 1988–89 season.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

===Philadelphia 76ers (1990–1993)===
On August 1, 1990, Golden State traded Bol to the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] for a 1991 first round draft pick ([[Chris Gatling]] was later selected).<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol's first tenure with the Philadelphia 76ers lasted three seasons, from 1990 to 1993. After playing in all 82 games in [[1990–91 NBA season|1990–91]], he played in 71 games the [[1991–92 NBA season|next season]] and in 58 games the [[1992–93 NBA season|following season]].<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/> During his last season in Philadelphia, he had a memorable night playing against former teammate [[Charles Barkley]] and the Phoenix Suns, making 6 of 12 three-pointers in the second half in a losing effort.<ref>{{cite web |title = Philadelphia 76ers at Phoenix Suns Box Score, March 3, 1993 |work = Basketball Reference.com |publisher = Sports Reference |url = https://www.basketball-reference.com/boxscores/PHO19930303.html |access-date = 2012-12-10 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071216132101/http://www.basketball-reference.com/boxscores/PHO19930303.html |archive-date = December 16, 2007 }}</ref> Fans were known to yell "shoot" as soon as Bol received the ball far from the basket.<ref>Kerry Eggers, "Around the League", The Sunday Oregonian, March 7, 1993</ref>

===Later career (1993–1997)===
After being released by Philadelphia in July 1993, Bol played in eight games in the [[1993–94 NBA season|1993–94 season]] with the [[Miami Heat]]. He scored only one two-point field goal with the team and blocked six shots in 61 total minutes.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

After being released by Miami on January 25, 1994, Bol played two games for the Washington Bullets in 1994 and then returned to Philadelphia, where he played four games.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

In October 1994, Bol returned to the Warriors. He played his last five NBA games there. On November 15, 1994, Bol came off of the bench to play 29 minutes against the Minnesota Timberwolves. He attempted three three-pointers in the fourth quarter and made them all.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/b/bolma01/gamelog/1995/|title=Manute Bol 1994–95 Game Log {{!}} Basketball-Reference.com|website=Basketball-Reference.com|language=en|access-date=2018-02-09}}</ref> Seven nights later in Charlotte, in a game nationally televised by [[Turner Network Television|TNT]], he was in the starting lineup again. By this time, two weeks into the season, his career seemed rejuvenated under Warrior head coach [[Don Nelson]]; he was again a defensive force, making threes and contributing as a starter to create matchup problems. After playing only ten minutes against the Hornets on November 22, 1994, he suffered a season-ending knee injury. Before he left the game, he recorded one block and two points and attempted a three-pointer in ten minutes of play.<ref name=":1" />{{better source needed|date=March 2024}} Bol was waived by Golden State on February 15, 1995.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/>

Bol played 22 games for the [[Florida Beach Dogs]] of the [[Continental Basketball Association]] during the 1995–96 season under Coach [[Eric Musselman]]. The Beach Dogs' games against the [[Sioux Falls Skyforce]] that season were broadcast by [[ESPN]], as the Skyforce also featured a former NBA player, [[Darryl Dawkins]].<ref name="SI 01"/>

In 1996, the [[Portland Wave|Portland Mountain Cats]] of the [[United States Basketball League]] announced that Bol would be playing with the team, but he never appeared in uniform.<ref name="SI 01"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://maineprosports.com/history-of-the-portland-mountain-cats/|title=History of the Portland Mountain Cats|date=February 24, 2019}}{{Dead link|date=December 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Bol played professionally in Italy in 1997 and in [[Qatar]] in 1998 before [[rheumatism]] forced him to retire permanently.<ref name="SI 01"/>

==Player profile and accomplishments==
Bol and [[Gheorghe Mureșan]] are the two tallest players in the history of the NBA.<ref name="Brown">{{cite book|last= Brown|first= Donald H.|title=A Basketball Handbook|year= 2007|publisher=AuthorHouse| isbn= 978-1-4259-6190-9| page=20|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YJmsqtj-rh4C&pg=PA20| location=Bloomington, Indiana}}</ref> Official NBA publications have listed Bol at either {{height|ft=7|in=6}}<ref name="MBNBA"/> or {{height|ft=7|in=7}}<ref name="NBAencyc"/> tall. He was measured by the [[Guinness Book of World Records]] at 7 ft 6 {{frac|3|4}} in tall.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kansascity.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/sam-mellinger/article5352999.html|title=Bol Bol, 14 years old and 6 feet 10, reaches for his father's heights|website=kansascity|access-date=7 February 2019}}</ref> Complementing his great height, Bol had exceptionally long limbs (inseam {{convert|49|in|cm}}) and large hands and feet ([[Shoe size|size]] 16 {{small|1/2}}). His [[arm span]], at {{convert|8|ft|6|in|m}}, is ({{as of|2023|lc=yes}}) the longest in NBA history, and his upward reach was {{convert|10|ft|5|in|m}}.<ref name="WaPo obit"/><ref>{{cite web |title = Former NBA player Manute Bol to speak at Union |publisher = Union College |date = Nov 3, 2008 |url = http://www.union.edu/N/DS/s.php?s=8105 |access-date = 2012-12-08 }}</ref>

With his great height and very long limbs, Bol was one of the NBA's most imposing defensive presences. Along with setting the rookie shot-blocking record in 1985–86, Bol later tied the NBA record for most blocked shots in one half (11) and in one quarter (eight, twice).<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title = Regular Season Records: Blocked Shots |encyclopedia = NBA Encyclopedia |publisher = National Basketball Association |url = http://www.nba.com/history/records/regular_blockedshots.html |access-date = 2012-12-10 }}</ref> On {{Dts|1992|January|31}}, in a game against the [[Orlando Magic]], he blocked four consecutive shots in a single possession.<ref name="FSN">{{cite episode |title = Manute Bol |series=Beyond the Glory |network = FOX Sports Net |airdate = Apr 17, 2005 }}</ref> On average, he blocked one shot per every 5.6 minutes of playing time.<ref name="SI 01">{{cite magazine |last = Anderson |first = Kelli |title = Manute Bol: Once the NBA's premier shot blocker, the Sudanese Sultan of Swat has tried to bring peace to his homeland |magazine = Sports Illustrated |date = Jul 2, 2001 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1022915/ |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140117043524/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1022915/ |url-status = dead |archive-date = January 17, 2014 }}</ref>
Bol's other basketball skills, however, were very limited. His rail-thin physique made it difficult for him to establish position against the league's bulkier centers and power forwards, and he also suffered from a [[Ulnar claw|claw hand]] on his right hand (his natural hand), which severely affected his shooting and ball-handling abilities. To compensate for this inherited deformity on his right hand, Bol learned to dribble, block shots and rebound with his (non-dominant) left hand.<ref>{{cite news |title=THE LONG LONELY JOURNEY OF MANUTE BOL YOU CAN TAKE THE BASKETBALL PLAYER OUT OF AFRICA, BUT YOU CAN'T TAKE THE AFRICA OUT OF THE BASKETBALL PLAYER |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212162801/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/magazine/1987/03/22/the-long-lonely-journey-of-manute-bol-you-can-take-the-basketball-player-out-of-africa-but-you-cant-take-the-africa-out-of-the-basketball-player/957c6862-1292-42e1-9c57-d043882e2c9a/ |archive-date=2023-02-12 |url-status=live |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/magazine/1987/03/22/the-long-lonely-journey-of-manute-bol-you-can-take-the-basketball-player-out-of-africa-but-you-cant-take-the-africa-out-of-the-basketball-player/957c6862-1292-42e1-9c57-d043882e2c9a/}}</ref>

Off the court, Bol established a reputation as a practical joker; Charles Barkley, a frequent victim of his pranks, has attested to Bol's sense of humor.<ref>{{cite web | last = Narducci | first = Marc | title = Tough Time for a Tall Guy His sense of humor could be a help to Manute Bol as he seeks to recover his health after a serious car crash. | publisher = Philly.com | date = Jul 8, 2005 | url = http://articles.philly.com/2004-07-18/sports/25371302_1_manute-bol-neville-h-robinson-sixers | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131114150123/http://articles.philly.com/2004-07-18/sports/25371302_1_manute-bol-neville-h-robinson-sixers | url-status = dead | archive-date = November 14, 2013 }}</ref>

In his NBA career, Bol averaged 2.6 points, 4.2 rebounds, 0.3 assists, and 3.3 blocks per game, playing an average of 18.7 minutes. He finished his career with 1,599 points, 2,647 rebounds, and 2,086 blocks. He appeared in 624 games over 10 seasons.<ref name="basketball-reference.com"/> As of 2019, Bol had the second-highest career blocks-per-game average (3.3) in the history of the NBA and was the only player in NBA history to have more blocked shots than points scored.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theringer.com/nba-draft/2019/6/19/18684291/bol-bol-oregon-manute-bol-nba-draft|title=Bol Bol Could Be a Whole New Kind of Basketball Player|first=Rodger|last=Sherman|date=June 19, 2019|website=The Ringer}}</ref>

==Humanitarian efforts and activism==
Bol was active in charitable causes during and after his basketball career. He claimed he spent much of the money he made during his NBA career supporting various causes relating to Sudan and its [[Second Sudanese Civil War|civil war]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Zumoff |first=Marc |title=Catching up with Manute Bol |journal=Drive |publisher=NBA Media Ventures |url=http://www.nba.com/sixers/features/drive_manute_bol_070807.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215162830/http://www.nba.com/sixers/features/drive_manute_bol_070807.html |archive-date=2007-12-15 }}</ref>

Bol frequently visited Sudanese refugee camps, where he was greeted enthusiastically by its inhabitants. In 2001 the Sudanese government offered him the post of minister of sport. Bol, a Christian,<ref>{{cite news |last = Shields |first = Jon A. |title = Manute Bol's radical Christianity |newspaper = The Wall Street Journal |date = Jun 25, 2010 |url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748704853404575323043046894012 }}</ref> refused because one of the conditions was converting to [[Islam]].<ref name="focusdep.com">{{cite web|last=Luo |first=Michael |title=NBA Star Now Refugee |agency=Associated Press |url=http://www.focusdep.com/articles/Society/NBA_Star_Now_Refugee |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070223041640/http://www.focusdep.com/articles/Society/NBA_Star_Now_Refugee |url-status=dead |archive-date=2007-02-23 }}</ref>

Later, the Sudanese government hindered Bol from leaving the country, accusing him of supporting the Dinka-led Christian rebels, the [[Sudan People's Liberation Army]]. It refused to grant him an exit visa unless he came back with more money. Assistance from supporters in the United States, including Senator [[Joe Lieberman]], raised money to provide Bol with plane tickets to Cairo, Egypt. After six months of negotiations with U.S. consulate officials regarding refugee status, Bol and his family were finally able to leave Egypt and return to the United States.<ref name="focusdep.com"/> He was admitted to the United States as a religious refugee in 2002 and settled in [[West Hartford, Connecticut]].<ref name="WaPo obit"/>

Bol established the [[Ring True Foundation]] to continue fund-raising for [[Sudanese refugees]]. He gave most of his earnings (an estimated $3.5 million) to their cause. In 2002, [[Fox TV]] agreed to broadcast the foundation's phone number in exchange for Bol's agreement to appear on their ''[[Celebrity Boxing]]'' show. After the referee goaded, "If you guys don't box, you won't get paid", he scored a third-round victory over former [[American football|football]] player [[William Perry (American football)|William "The Refrigerator" Perry]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL 100 |url=https://www.nfl.com/100/originals/100-greatest/characters-23 |access-date=2024-07-08 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Height wins fights in ''Celebrity Boxing II'' |url=https://ew.com/article/2002/05/23/height-wins-fights-celebrity-boxing-ii/ |access-date=2024-07-08 |website=EW.com |language=en}}</ref>

In late 2002, Bol signed a one-day contract with the [[Indianapolis Ice]] of the [[Central Hockey League]]. Though he could not skate, the publicity generated by his single-game appearance helped raise money to assist children in Sudan.<ref>{{cite book|first=Jon C.|last=Scott|title=Hockey Night in Dixie: Minor Pro Hockey in the American South|year=2006|publisher=Heritage House Publishing Company Ltd.|page=[https://archive.org/details/hockeynightindix0000stot/page/184 184]|isbn=1-894974-21-2|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/hockeynightindix0000stot}}</ref>

Bol was involved in the April 2006 [[Sudan Freedom Walk]], a three-week march from the [[United Nations]] building in New York City to the [[United States Capitol]] in Washington, DC. The event was organized by [[Simon Deng]], a former Sudanese swimming champion who was a longtime friend of Bol's. Deng, who was enslaved from age 9 to 12, is from another tribe in Southern Sudan. His Sudan Freedom Walk focused on finding a solution to the [[genocide]] in [[Darfur]] (western Sudan) but also sought to raise awareness of the modern-day slavery and human-rights abuses throughout Sudan. Bol spoke in New York City at the start of the walk, and in [[Philadelphia]] at a rally organized by former hunger striker [[Nathan Kleinman]].{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Center of two worlds |url=}}</ref>

Bol was also an advocate for reconciliation efforts, and worked to improve education in South Sudan. A Nicholas Kristof article<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/24/opinion/24kristof.html?_r=3&ref=nicholasdkristof |newspaper=The New York Times |first=Nicholas D. |last=Kristof |title=Most Valuable Helper |date=Jun 23, 2010}}</ref> in ''The New York Times'' highlighted Bol's work for reconciliation and education with an organization called [[Sudan Sunrise]]. Bol first began working with Sudan Sunrise to raise awareness on issues of reconciliation in 2005. This included speaking at the United States Capitol and subsequently partnering with Sudan Sunrise to build schools across South Sudan that, in the spirit of reconciliation, would enroll students regardless of tribe or religion.<ref>{{cite web |title = Manute Bol School |work = Current Projects in South Sudan |publisher = Sudan Sunrise |url = https://www.sudansunrise.org/project/manute-bol-school |access-date = 2012-12-14 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Bol had six children with his first wife, Atong, and four with his second wife, Ajok.<ref>{{cite news |last = McGeehan |first = Patrick |title = Manute Bol, N.B.A. Player and Activist, Dies at 47 |newspaper = The New York Times |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/20/sports/basketball/20bol.html?scp=2 }}</ref> Bol's son Madut (born December 19, 1989) played college basketball at [[Southern Jaguars basketball|Southern University]] and graduated in 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/basketball/nba/2010-06-29-manute-bol-funeral_N.htm|title=Manute Bol remembered as 'also a giant off the court' at funeral|date=June 29, 2010|work=USA Today|access-date=March 23, 2014}}</ref> Another son, [[Bol Bol]] (born November 16, 1999), is an NBA basketball player.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.si.com/nba/suns/analysis/bol-bol-brings-phoenix-suns-stacked-roster|title=What Bol Bol Brings to Stacked Suns Roster|first=Everett|last=Williams|date=July 17, 2023|magazine=Sports Illustrated }}</ref> Bol was [[Catholic Church|Catholic]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Manute Bol Honored as a Moral, Spiritual Giant |url=https://communications.catholic.edu//news/2010/11/manute.doc.html |access-date=2022-11-25 |website=The Catholic University of America |language=en}}</ref>

Bol spoke [[Dinka language|Dinka]] and [[Arabic language|Arabic]] before learning English.<ref>{{cite magazine |last = Lidz |first = Franz |title = Come See The Dinka Dunker Do: Manute Bol, an import from Sudan, is giving a 7'6" lift to Bridgeport |magazine = Sports Illustrated |date = Dec 10, 1984 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1122922/ |archive-url = https://archive.today/20130119145546/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1122922/ |url-status = dead |archive-date = January 19, 2013 }}</ref>

In July 1988, Bol was arrested for driving while intoxicated and resisting arrest. On August 28, 1988, Bol was arrested in Maryland for driving while intoxicated.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1988/08/29/former-bullets-player-manute-bol-arrested-again/21085cff-a96c-49ce-b19b-2a2662d9aeb1/|title=FORMER BULLETS PLAYER MANUTE BOL ARRESTED AGAIN |newspaper=Washington Post |last=Priest |first=Dana |date=August 28, 1988}}</ref>

Despite initially knowing little English or Western culture upon arriving in the United States, Bol adjusted and was widely regarded as well-rounded, inquisitive, and well-read. He developed a strong friendship with Charles Barkley, who remarked, "If everyone in the world was a Manute Bol, it's a world I'd want to live in. He's smart. He reads ''The New York Times''. He knows what's going on in a lot of subjects. He's not one of these just-basketball guys".<ref name="SI 90">{{cite magazine |last = Montville |first = Leigh |title = A Tall Story: Manute Bol, the Sixers' 7'7" center, views life from a unique perspective |magazine = Sports Illustrated |date = Dec 17, 1990 |url = http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1136052/ |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140117173345/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1136052/ |url-status = dead |archive-date = January 17, 2014 }}</ref>

During his time in Egypt, Bol ran a basketball school in [[Cairo]]. One of his pupils was a fellow Sudanese refugee, future NBA player [[Luol Deng]], the son of a former Sudanese cabinet minister. Deng later moved to the United States to further his basketball career, maintaining a close relationship with Bol.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/page/blackhistoryNBA1|title=Wallace: Luol Deng's path of righteousness|date=26 February 2015|website=ESPN.com}}</ref>

On February 11, 2004, Bol was arrested in West Hartford, Connecticut for assault, disorderly conduct, and interfering with a police officer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=1734393|title=Manute Bol arrested for hitting daughter|date=February 13, 2004|website=ESPN.com}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.courant.com/2004/02/13/town-news-briefing-4728/|title=TOWN NEWS BRIEFING|date=February 13, 2004|website=courant.com}}</ref> Police alleged that Bol had struck his daughter and injured her lip. According to the ''[[Hartford Courant]]'', Bol was intoxicated and also attempted to harm himself. He received medical treatment for his injuries following the incident.<ref name="auto"/>

In July 2004, Bol was seriously injured in a car accident in [[Colchester, Connecticut]]; he was ejected from a taxi that hit a guardrail and overturned, resulting in a broken neck.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Fox|first1=Tracy Gordon|last2=Farrell|first2=Jim|title=Bol critically injured in car accident|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1914&dat=20040702&id=GxAqAAAAIBAJ&pg=1174,283134|access-date=8 July 2014|work=The Hartford Courant|date=2 July 2014}}</ref> The driver, who died following the accident, was driving with a suspended license<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/news/story?id=1845646|title=Report: Bol's driver had suspended license|date=July 24, 2004|website=ESPN.com}}</ref> and was intoxicated.<ref name="auto4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=2347196|title=Bol, wife arrested, charged with disorderly conduct|date=February 27, 2006|website=ESPN.com}}</ref> Because his fortunes were mostly donated to Sudan and he had no health insurance, Bol was financially ruined by the accident.<ref name="FSN"/> Bol was hospitalized for three months following the accident.<ref name="auto4"/> When he recovered from his injuries, he moved to [[Olathe, Kansas]].<ref name="WaPo obit"/>

On February 26, 2006, Bol and his wife Ajok were both arrested in West Harford, Connecticut following a physical altercation at their home.<ref name="auto4"/>

==Death==
On June 19, 2010, Bol died from [[acute kidney failure]] and complications from [[Stevens–Johnson syndrome]] at the [[University of Virginia Health System|University of Virginia Medical Center]] in [[Charlottesville, Virginia]].<ref name="WaPo obit">{{cite news|last=Schudel|first=Matt |title=Manute Bol, former Washington Bullet and one of NBA's tallest players, dies at 47|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/19/AR2010061902214.html|access-date=19 June 2010|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=19 June 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.pitch.com/plog/2010/06/manute_bol_retired_basketball_player_has_died.php |title=Manute Bol, retired basketball player, has died |last=Kendall |first=Justin |date=June 19, 2010 |access-date=2010-06-19 |publisher=The Pitch |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100622032557/http://blogs.pitch.com/plog/2010/06/manute_bol_retired_basketball_player_has_died.php |archive-date=June 22, 2010 }}</ref> He is buried in [[South Sudan]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kmbc.com/news/24214449/detail.html|title=Memorial To Honor Manute Bol|access-date=27 August 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307131045/http://www.kmbc.com/news/24214449/detail.html|archive-date=7 March 2012}}</ref>

===Funeral service and tributes===
[[File:Manute Bol's funeral at National Cathedral 2010-06-29 1.jpg|thumb|Bol's memorial service at the [[Washington National Cathedral]]]]

Bol's memorial service was held on June 29, 2010, at the [[Washington National Cathedral]] in Washington, DC. His body lay in an eight-foot-long, specially-built casket.<ref name="google.com">{{cite web |url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/canadianpress/article/ALeqM5j4CZIgXsXmROD8dYFKNNhS3BpA2w |title=Unknown |access-date=June 7, 2024}}{{dead link|date=June 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> At the funeral, U.S. Senator [[Sam Brownback]] said, "I can't think of a person that I know of in the world [who] used [his] celebrity status for a greater good than what Manute Bol did. He did it for his people. He gave his life for his people." NBA Development Vice President [[Rory Sparrow]] added, "'He had a heart that was very large and full of compassion for his fellow man'".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/sports/manute-bol-a-life-of-faith-courage-and-moral-dignity/1871846/|title=Manute Bol: A "Life of Faith, Courage and Moral Dignity"|website=NBC Washington |date=June 30, 2010}}</ref>

After his death, tributes to Bol's career and charitable works came from around the United States and the world.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/gallery/2010/06/19/GA2010061902220.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110131134124/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/gallery/2010/06/19/GA2010061902220.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=2011-01-31 |newspaper=The Washington Post|title=Manute Bol, former Washington Bullet: 1962–2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://archive.boston.com/sports/basketball/articles/2010/06/22/manute_bol_had_height_of_course_but_even_more_depth/ |work=The Boston Globe |title=Height, and depth |first=Bob |last=Ryan |date=June 22, 2010}}</ref> His former teams, and the NBA, issued statements in recognition of his impact on the sport of basketball and on Sudan.<ref>{{cite web |last = Leonsis |first = Ted |title = Ted Leonsis' Statement on Passing of Manute Bol |work = Washington Wizards news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = https://www.nba.com/wizards/news/bol_100619.html |access-date = 2012-12-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title = Former Warrior Manute Bol Passes Away |work = Golden State Warriors news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = http://www.nba.com/warriors/news/bol_passes_away_061810.html |access-date = 2012-12-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last = Stefanski |first = Ed |title = Philadelphia 76ers statement on the passing of Manute Bol |work = Philadelphia 76ers news |publisher = NBA Media Ventures |date = Jun 19, 2010 |url = http://www.nba.com/sixers/news/bol_100619.html |access-date = 2012-12-14 }}</ref> Brownback paid tribute to Bol on the floor of the United States Senate.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/video/2010/06/22/VI2010062202905.html |newspaper=The Washington Post |title=Video: A Senate salute to Manute |date=2010-06-22}}</ref>

The team sponsored a giveaway of 10,000 of the tallest bobbleheads in franchise history, at {{convert|10|inches|cm}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://abc7news.com/sports/warriors-honor-manute-bol-with-bobblehead/493801/|title=Warriors honor Manute Bol with bobblehead|date=28 January 2015|website=ABC7 San Francisco}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nba.com/warriors/news/manute-bol-bobblehead-night-20150127|title=Warriors to Host Manute Bol Bobblehead Night on Tuesday, January 27 Against the Chicago Bulls|website=Golden State Warriors}}</ref>
* The "Manute Bol Court" was built and constructed in South Sudan by the Luol Deng Foundation in 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://beyondsport.org/articles/the-loul-deng-foundation-opens-the-manute-bol-court-in-south-sudan/|title=Beyond Sport|website=beyondsport.org|access-date=March 10, 2019|archive-date=December 9, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231209134438/https://beyondsport.org/articles/the-loul-deng-foundation-opens-the-manute-bol-court-in-south-sudan/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sportingnews.com/us/nba/news/luol-deng-manute-bol-court-south-sudan-picture-instagram/xyqo3igvj66m1x24pfclvaw23|title=Luol Deng: South Sudan court among 'most memorable' accomplishments|date=10 August 2015|website=Sporting News}}</ref>
* The Manute Bol Peace Builders Basketball Tournament is held annually throughout Sudan.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.voanews.com/a/south-sudan-organizes-manute-bol-basketball-tournament/2828742.html|title=Basketball Tournament Honors Manute Bol|website=VOA|date=June 19, 2015 }}</ref>
* In 2016, Bol was inducted into the [[Fairfield County, Connecticut|Fairfield County]] Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sudansunrise.org/fairfield-county-hall-fame-honors-manute-bol/|title=Fairfield County Hall of Fame Honors Manute Bol|date=19 October 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.greenwichtime.com/sports/article/Sports-Night-dinner-honors-Hall-of-Fame-inductees-9979373.php|title=Sports Night dinner honors Hall of Fame inductees|first=David|last=Fierro|date=18 October 2016|website=GreenwichTime|access-date=March 10, 2019|archive-date=February 12, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212162820/https://www.greenwichtime.com/sports/article/Sports-Night-dinner-honors-Hall-of-Fame-inductees-9979373.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>
